@graph.name: How to Hire a Chatbot Developer — 6-Step Guide
@graph.description: Step-by-step guide to evaluating and hiring a qualified LLM chatbot developer for your business.

step.name: Define your chatbot use case
step.text: Identify the specific job the chatbot must do: answer support questions, qualify leads, book appointments, or process transactions. Narrow scope delivers faster, higher-quality results.

step.name: Assess your knowledge base readiness
step.text: Gather your documentation, support articles, product FAQs, and policies. A RAG chatbot is only as good as its knowledge base — poor documentation produces poor chatbot answers.

step.name: Evaluate developer's RAG experience
step.text: Ask the developer to explain their RAG pipeline architecture: embedding model choice, vector database, chunking strategy, and retrieval evaluation with RAGAS. Any developer who can't explain this is not qualified.

step.name: Review their hallucination mitigation approach
step.text: Ask specifically: 'How do you prevent hallucinations in production?' The answer should include: source citations, confidence thresholds, output validation, and RAGAS evaluation metrics.

step.name: Verify platform integration experience
step.text: For your target platforms (Slack, Teams, WhatsApp, web widget), ask for examples of previous integrations. Platform-specific requirements (Block Kit, Adaptive Cards, WABA approval) require experience.

step.name: Agree on evaluation criteria before launch
step.text: Define success: minimum RAGAS scores, escalation rate targets, response latency limits, and cost-per-conversation budget. A professional developer will have pre-launch evaluation checklists.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a RAG chatbot and a fine-tuned LLM chatbot?

acceptedAnswer.text: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): the LLM is unchanged; answers are grounded by retrieving relevant documents from your knowledge base at inference time. Advantages: knowledge can be updated instantly, answers cite sources, significantly cheaper than fine-tuning. Fine-tuning: the LLM's weights are updated with domain-specific training data. Better for capturing stylistic patterns, but expensive ($500–$5,000+ per run), knowledge goes stale without retraining, and the model can still hallucinate. For 99% of business chatbot use cases: RAG is the right choice.

mainEntity.name: How does a chatbot developer handle LLM cost management in production?

acceptedAnswer.text: Key strategies: (1) Model selection — use GPT-4o-mini or Claude Haiku for simple FAQs; reserve GPT-4o/Claude 3.5 for complex reasoning. (2) Context window optimization — summarize older turns rather than include full history. (3) Semantic caching — cache near-identical queries with Redis + embedding similarity. (4) Token monitoring — instrument every LLM call with input/output token counts. (5) Rate limits — cap per-user conversations to prevent abuse. Target: $0.01–$0.05 per conversation for standard customer support chatbots.

mainEntity.name: What deliverables should I expect from a chatbot development project?

acceptedAnswer.text: A professional chatbot delivery package includes: (1) Source code deposited to your GitHub repository. (2) Architecture document with system design and data flow. (3) Knowledge base setup with vector database and chunking documentation. (4) Analytics dashboard showing conversations, escalation rate, accuracy, and cost. (5) RAGAS evaluation report with faithfulness, relevance, and context recall scores. (6) Platform deployment on all agreed channels. (7) Admin panel for your team to update the knowledge base. (8) Runbook for monitoring and maintenance. (9) 60-day bug warranty.

mainEntity.name: Can a chatbot developer build an agent that takes actions, not just answers questions?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — AI agents use tools: search the web, query a database, send emails, create calendar events, call APIs. LangChain or LangGraph orchestrates the agent loop — the LLM decides which tool to call based on the user's request. Examples: customer service agent that processes returns (not just answers); HR agent that books leave directly in the system; sales agent that creates CRM records. The complexity and cost of building an agent is higher than a pure chatbot — verify whether answering questions or taking actions is the actual requirement before committing to agent architecture.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take to build a production-ready chatbot?

acceptedAnswer.text: Timeline by complexity: (1) Simple FAQ chatbot — 1–2 weeks. (2) Customer support chatbot with RAG and Zendesk escalation — 3–4 weeks. (3) Multi-platform chatbot (web + Slack + Teams + WhatsApp) — 5–8 weeks. (4) Voice-enabled chatbot — add 2–3 weeks. (5) AI agent with tool use — 6–10 weeks. Timeline accelerators: clean documentation on day one; 100+ representative test questions prepared; single decision-maker for approvals; 24-hour feedback turnaround during UAT.
